clue.text: Louis d'or? It hasn't been in circulation for years in this part of the world

definitions.text: Louis d'or? It hasn't been in circulation for years in this part of the world

parts.words: Louis d'or? It hasn't been in circulation for years in this part of the world
parts.note: the French gold coin prompts its British counterpart, a gold coin worth a pound that no longer passes from hand to hand here

explanation.surface: A collector muses on an old French coin no longer spent locally.
explanation.walkthrough: The Louis d'or was a French gold coin; the British equivalent in 'this part of the world' is the gold one-pound coin, long out of everyday use.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are historic gold coins, the British one a pound piece that stopped being everyday currency long ago.

clue.text: Remarks made about nothing in particular

definitions.text: Remarks made about nothing in particular

parts.words: Remarks made about nothing in particular
parts.note: remarks that cover things broadly rather than any particular case; the surface suggests idle small talk

explanation.walkthrough: 'About nothing in particular' sounds like idle chatter, but it means statements that do not concern any specific instance.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad statements apply to whole classes of things rather than to any specific case.

clue.text: Catching and getting in fish

indicators.note: one word catching another holds it inside, so the fish word encloses the conjunction

parts.note: a ling is a long sea fish of the cod family
taken as written

explanation.surface: An angler's day of catching and hauling in fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting in fish' looks like one phrase, but 'fish' is LING, which catches AND; 'getting in' alone is the definition, as an aircraft gets in to land.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft or traveller arriving at a destination is touching down there.

clue.text: Extremely irritable

parts.note: a nervy, tense temper, with 'Extremely' hinting at the outermost border of something

explanation.definitionFit: A tense, jumpy person is on a knife's border, quick to snap.

clue.text: Unintellectual impression about sunburst

indicators.note: the stamp word goes round the scrambled letters, as one thing placed about another

parts.note: a seal is an impression stamped in wax

indicators.note: something burst is broken apart, so the letters of sun are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a painting of a sunburst as shallow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sunburst' reads as one word, but 'burst' signals an anagram of 'sun', which 'about' puts inside the stamp.
explanation.definitionFit: Something appealing to the physical senses rather than the mind is the opposite of cerebral.

clue.text: I invest in two types of vessel for the papal authority

indicators.note: to invest in is to put something into, so the letter goes inside the pair of containers

parts.note: a vat is a large tank for liquids
a can is a metal container

explanation.surface: Someone puts money into two kinds of ship to serve the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests ships, but here both types are containers, a tank and a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy See, government of the Roman Catholic Church, is named after its seat in Rome.

clue.text: About a thousand sheets of paper? No, roughly half that

definitions.text: sheets of paper? No, roughly half that

parts.note: re means about or concerning
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Someone guesses a thousand sheets of paper and is corrected to about five hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: The first words look like part of the definition, but 'About a thousand' is the wordplay; the definition says the bundle is roughly half of a thousand sheets, i.e. 480 or 500.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard bundle of paper holds 480 or 500 sheets, about half a thousand.

clue.text: Italian money returned to a goblin put in jeopardy

parts.note: an imp is a small mischievous sprite

indicators.note: coming back means the currency word is read backwards

parts.note: the lira (plural lire) was Italy's currency before the euro

explanation.surface: A goblin given back Italian cash finds himself in danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reads the old Italian currency backwards, and 'to a goblin' puts it after the sprite.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger something is to expose it to risk.

clue.text: Short of a length? Decidedly!

parts.note: the question suggests cricket bowling falling short, but the emphatic reply describes something extremely close, with no gap whatever

explanation.walkthrough: 'Short of a length' is a cricket term for a ball pitched shorter than a good length; here it means having no length at all, i.e. very close by.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase for extreme nearness, implying zero separation between places.

clue.text: Deserted racecourse with more than eight corners?

definitions.text: Deserted racecourse with more than eight corners?

parts.words: Deserted racecourse with more than eight corners?
parts.note: a racecourse with no horse running on it, split into three short words, describes a nine-sided figure

explanation.walkthrough: A deserted racecourse has 'no nag on' it; run together, those words name a shape with nine corners, one more than eight.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane figure with nine angles and nine sides.

clue.text: Edward, restraining the inclination, went hiking

indicators.note: one word restraining another holds it in, so the name encloses the slope

parts.note: Ted is a short form of Edward
a ramp is an inclined slope

explanation.surface: Edward, holding back his preference, set off on a walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inclination' suggests a preference, but here it is a slope, which the short name for Edward holds.
explanation.definitionFit: To walk heavily over a long distance is to trek on foot.

clue.text: Men trained to shoot in wet weather

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, soldiers trained to fire guns; the answer also sitting in 'trained' is a coincidence
taken as written

explanation.surface: Soldiers are drilled in firing during a downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for the Royal Artillery, the British army's gunners.
explanation.definitionFit: Precipitation falling as drops is the classic damp weather.

clue.text: Dead slow? Quite the contrary!

parts.note: the word wanted is the opposite of both dead and slow: living, as in the old phrase pairing the living with the dead, and also fast

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead slow' is a nautical order for minimum speed; the opposite of 'dead' in the old sense is 'living' (as in 'the quick and the dead'), and of 'slow' is 'fast'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both fast and, archaically, alive.

clue.text: Essential equipment for invaders from mars

indicators.note: the answer is made from the letters of the planet's name, rearranged

explanation.surface: Martians come equipped with weapons for their invasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' signals that the letters of MARS are rearranged to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Invading forces need weapons above all.

clue.text: Throw away a fight

explanation.definitionFit: To discard something as useless; also a brief brawl.

clue.text: Silver-headed sort of owl tingling with warmth

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, placed at the head of the answer

indicators.note: a sort of owl is a rearranged version of the word, so its letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A silver-crested owl glows warmly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'headed' puts AG, silver's chemical symbol, first; 'sort of' rearranges OWL to LOW.
explanation.definitionFit: Glowing with heat or emotion, flushed and radiant.

clue.text: Rational U S soldiers entering a neighbourly tavern

indicators.note: one item entering another goes inside it, so the soldiers go into the pub word

parts.note: a local is one's nearby pub
GI is a common term for an American soldier

explanation.surface: Sensible American troops walk into the nearby pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'local' is British slang for the pub nearest one's home.
explanation.definitionFit: Following sound reasoning; sensible and coherent.

clue.text: A flower that offers everything, for example, in retrospect

indicators.note: looking back in retrospect means the run of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: all means everything

explanation.surface: A bloom said to give you everything, looking back.
explanation.walkthrough: ALL + EG + IN, read backwards as 'retrospect' signals, gives the answer; 'that offers' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Love-in-a-mist is a garden plant of this genus with blue blooms.

clue.text: Is least disposed to weigh anchor

indicators.note: disposed here means arranged differently, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is the least inclined to start a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposed' looks like 'inclined', but it signals that IS LEAST is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising the anchor is what a ship does when departing on a voyage.

clue.text: One as yet far too young to take certain steps

definitions.text: One as yet far too young to take certain steps

parts.words: One as yet far too young to take certain steps
parts.note: suggests someone too young for big life decisions, but really a small child whose steps are still unsteady

explanation.walkthrough: 'Certain steps' suggests serious decisions, but it means sure-footed steps, which a small child just learning to walk cannot yet take.
explanation.definitionFit: A child aged roughly one to three who walks unsteadily.

clue.text: Incorrect ruling for a Rugby formation?

parts.note: a line is a ruled stroke on paper
out means wrong, as in a calculation that is out

explanation.surface: A referee's wrong decision about a rugby set-piece.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby union this is the restart where forwards line up and the ball is thrown in from touch.
explanation.definitionFit: The set piece in which players form parallel ranks to contest a throw from touch.

clue.text: Dull publicity men I finally take into account

parts.note: PR men, public relations staff, are pros

indicators.note: to take something into another is to put it inside, so the letter goes within the abbreviation

explanation.surface: Dull PR men whom I eventually bring into consideration.
explanation.walkthrough: AC is the usual short form of account; 'take into' sets I within it, and 'finally' only says this comes at the end of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking imagination or excitement; ordinary and flat.

clue.text: Like any drink that can be pocketed, we hear?

indicators.note: says the answer is spoken like the word for pocketable

parts.note: a ball that can be potted, as in snooker, is pottable

explanation.surface: A drink you could slip into your pocket, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker to 'pot' a ball is to sink it into a pocket, so 'pottable' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Safe or fit to drink, as any beverage should be.

clue.text: He flies a 6 over a rocky height

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A pilot flies over a rugged hill.
explanation.walkthrough: '6' looks like a cross-reference to 6-down, but it is just the number six, VI.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot is the person who flies an aircraft.

clue.text: The ebb and flow of French follows it back

indicators.note: the French word follows, so it is placed after the reversed piece
read back means the little word is reversed

parts.note: taken as written
de is French for of

explanation.surface: The rise and fall of the French tongue follows its own course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the little word round, and the French for 'of' follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: The regular rise and fall of the sea.

clue.text: Can turn into American fighting formations

indicators.note: one piece put into another goes inside it, so the reversed container sits in the country abbreviation
turning a word reverses its letters

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: Containers transformed into American combat groups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb, but it is TIN; 'turn' reverses it to NIT, placed into US.
explanation.definitionFit: Military groups such as companies and battalions.

clue.text: One god in India, but four in South Africa

indicators.note: the numeral goes in the country's abbreviation

parts.note: IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A deity is single in India yet fourfold in South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'but' contrast is surface; the god is also spelt Shiva.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hindu destroyer god, one of the principal deities.

clue.text: A card-game that's simple to break off

definitions.meaning: a children's game of matching cards
something easy, as in 'it's a cinch'
to crack or come apart suddenly

explanation.definitionFit: A matching card game for children; also something easy; also to break sharply.

clue.text: The Bear River in the States?

indicators.note: the river abbreviation goes inside the country's abbreviation

parts.note: USA is the United States

explanation.surface: A bear spotted by an American river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' suggests a beast, but it is the Latin name of the constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin name for a bear, given to the constellations Major and Minor.

clue.text: Shakespearean exponent of courtly or country love

parts.note: taken as written
a land is a country
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare character expresses refined or rustic romance.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition stops at 'courtly': the lovesick hero of As You Like It; the rest is OR + LAND + O.
explanation.definitionFit: The ardent lover of Rosalind in As You Like It.

clue.text: A bitter brew that may go to a clergyman's head

definitions.text: may go to a clergyman's head

indicators.note: brewing mixes ingredients, so the letters of the two words are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A bitter beer might go straight to a vicar's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go to a clergyman's head' sounds like drink making him tipsy, but it means headwear worn by clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: A square cap worn by Roman Catholic clergy.

clue.text: Utilise one's last resources to get the inside of a gun clean?

definitions.meaning: to make do with whatever poor remains are left

definitions.text: get the inside of a gun clean?
definitions.meaning: to scour the bore of a firearm

explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for using the last poor options; literally, scouring a gun's bore.
